prime.problem: Real lifetimes age: a rat exposed to radiation, a bearing, a disk. An exponential says an old part is as good as new, which is wrong for anything that wears out. You need a lifetime model whose risk can rise with age, plus a way to get its mean without an integral that has no elementary antiderivative.
prime.fits: It generalises the exponential card (shape k = 1) by letting the hazard change with age, and reuses its tail trick. The source files it under "Gamma"; the gamma distribution itself (a sum of exponentials) returns in the CLT card.
expect: Weibull shape k and scale λ
the gamma function Γ(z) and Γ(z + 1) = zΓ(z)
hazard that falls, stays flat or rises
Gamma(α, θ) as a sum of α exponentials
prime.goal: Compute any Weibull survival probability and moment from one substitution, explain what the shape parameter does to the hazard, and tell the Weibull and the gamma distribution apart.

attend: Why does the substitution y = (x/120)³ make f(x) dx collapse to e<sup>−y</sup> dy?
Which power of y appears in the mean's integral, and how does that pick out Γ(4/3)?
Why is the rat's mean 107.16 weeks and not the scale 120, and for which k would they be equal?
What does the hazard ratio (150/50)² = 9 tell you about a shape-3 lifetime?
Why does the source's heading say Gamma when the gamma distribution never appears?

must: S(x) = e<sup>−(x/λ)<sup>k</sup></sup> → substitute y = (x/λ)<sup>k</sup> → the density becomes e<sup>−y</sup> dy → survival is one exponential: P(X > 100) = e<sup>−125/216</sup> = 0.5606

Mean = ∫ x f(x) dx with x = λy<sup>1/k</sup> → ∫ λy<sup>1/k</sup>e<sup>−y</sup> dy → matches Γ(z) with z = 1 + 1/k → E[X<sup>n</sup>] = λ<sup>n</sup>Γ(1 + n/k): every moment from one line (107.16, sd 38.95)

Hazard h(x) = (k/λ)(x/λ)<sup>k−1</sup> → k > 1 rises with age, k = 1 flat (exponential), k < 1 falls → the shape parameter is the modelling choice about ageing, and one Weibull can't fit a bathtub curve
elevated: Γ(z + 1) = zΓ(z) → Γ(4/3) = Γ(1/3)/3 = 0.8930 → non-integer shapes still give closed-form moments via math.gamma, so no scipy and no numerical integration

compress.prompt: Write the substitution and the two results it gives (survival and the n-th moment) from memory. Then draw three hazard curves for k < 1, k = 1, k > 1 and label which is the exponential.
checklist: y = (x/λ)<sup>k</sup> turns f(x) dx into e<sup>−y</sup> dy
E[X<sup>n</sup>] = λ<sup>n</sup>Γ(1 + n/k); the mean equals λ only when k = 1
k sets the hazard's direction; k = 1 is memoryless
Gamma distribution = sum of exponentials; it shares only the Γ function and the k = α = 1 case

retrieve.q: Explain why the rat's mean lifetime is below the scale parameter 120 weeks.
answer: 63.2% of rats die before the scale for every k
for k = 3 deaths cluster just below 120 (mode 104.8) with little long tail
so the mean is 120 Γ(4/3) = 107.16, less than 120; only k = 1 gives mean = scale

retrieve.q: Walk through deriving E[X] for the rat, from the integral to the number, naming each substitution and identity.
answer: E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx; set y = (x/120)³, so x = 120y<sup>1/3</sup> and f(x) dx = e<sup>−y</sup> dy

retrieve.q: You have failure times for a part. Choose between exponential, Weibull and gamma, and say what evidence would push you to each.
answer: exponential if the hazard looks flat (log-survival is a straight line)
Weibull if the hazard rises or falls steadily with age
gamma if failure is the α-th of several random shocks
none alone if the hazard is bathtub-shaped: fit phases separately or go nonparametric

compare.q: Put the rat (k = 3) next to an exponential with the same scale 120. What differs in P(X > 100), in the hazard at 50 vs 150 weeks, and in which one is memoryless?
answer: hazard: 0.00434 → 0.03906 (9×) for the rat, flat 1/120 = 0.00833 for the exponential
only the exponential is memoryless; the rat's risk rises, so an old rat is worse than a young one

compare.q: The gamma distribution is a sum of α exponentials; the CLT card sums 20 jobs. What does the gamma give you exactly that the CLT only approximates, and when does it matter?
answer: the gamma is the exact law of a sum of exponentials, including its skew
the CLT keeps only the mean and variance and assumes a symmetric bell
it matters in the tails: the card's gamma check gave 0.0106 against the CLT's 0.0127 for A.J. under 900

predict.q: Keep the rat's scale at 120 weeks but make the shape k = 1/2. Before computing: will the mean be above or below 120, and will the hazard at 150 weeks be higher or lower than at 50?
predict.answer: Above, and lower. The mean is 120 Γ(1 + 2) = 120 × 2! = 240 weeks: a falling hazard means most die early but a few survive very long, dragging the mean out. With k < 1 the hazard (k/λ)(x/λ)<sup>k−1</sup> falls with age, so a rat that has survived to 150 weeks is at lower risk than one at 50.

apply.task: Rework the rat with shape k = 2 (scale still 120): compute P(X > 100), E[X] and the median by hand using the substitution and math.gamma. Then say whether the hazard at 150 weeks is higher or lower than at 50, and by what factor.
apply.done: You have P(X > 100) = e<sup>−(5/6)²</sup> = e<sup>−0.6944</sup> = 0.4994, E[X] = 120 Γ(3/2) = 106.35, median 120 √(ln 2) = 99.91, and a hazard ratio of 150/50 = 3 (it grows like x<sup>k−1</sup> = x).
